purpose: Apomorphine is used to help people with Parkinson's disease during sudden 'off' episodes — times when their regular medication stops working and they experience stiffness, tremors, or trouble moving. It works quickly to get you moving again. It is not a cure, but it helps manage these unpredictable freezing spells.
how_it_works: In Parkinson's disease, the brain does not make enough of a chemical called dopamine, which helps control movement. Apomorphine acts like dopamine in your brain, stepping in to fill that role and help your muscles move more smoothly. It works very fast — usually within 10 to 20 minutes — making it great for sudden episodes.
common_side_effects: Nausea and vomiting (very common — you will likely be given an anti-nausea pill ahead of time), dizziness or lightheadedness especially when standing up, sleepiness, injection site reactions like redness or soreness, runny nose, and yawning.
warnings: This medication can cause a serious drop in blood pressure, especially when you stand up — sit or stand slowly to avoid falls. It can cause sudden severe sleepiness, even while doing things like driving, so use caution. Never mix apomorphine with anti-nausea medications called 5HT3 antagonists (like ondansetron) as this combination can cause dangerously low blood pressure. Avoid alcohol. Tell your doctor if you have heart problems or kidney disease.
typical_dosing: Apomorphine comes as an injection (Apokyn) given just under the skin, or as a film (Kynmobi) placed under the tongue. The injection is usually started at a low dose of 2 mg and slowly adjusted by your doctor — typical doses range from 2 mg to 6 mg per episode. The under-the-tongue film usually starts at 10 mg per episode. It is used only as needed during 'off' episodes, not on a regular schedule, and generally no more than 5 times a day.
